questions.subtopic: OSI vs TCP/IP Reference Model. Layer Mapping
questions.question: An IS auditor maps controls documented in TCP/IP terms to the OSI model. Which OSI layers does the TCP/IP application layer MOST closely cover?

options.A: Transport, session and application layers together
options.B: Physical and data link layers of the model
options.C: Session, presentation and application layers
options.D: Network and transport layers of the model

questions.key_concept: The TCP/IP application layer combines the OSI session, presentation and application layers; transport remains a separate layer in both models.
questions.pre_read: Count the layers in each model. Ask which OSI layers have no separate TCP/IP counterpart.
questions.correct_explanation: The TCP/IP model folds the top three OSI layers (session, presentation and application) into its single application layer. Transport is a separate layer in both models, which is why the closest alternative fails: it pulls the OSI transport layer into the application layer, although TCP and UDP sit in a TCP/IP transport layer of their own.

wrong_explanations.A: Session and application do sit in the TCP/IP application layer. Map layers by function, though: end-to-end delivery is a job of its own.
wrong_explanations.B: Physical and data link functions map to the TCP/IP link layer at the bottom of the stack, not the application layer.
wrong_explanations.D: Network and transport functions map to the TCP/IP internet and transport layers, which sit below the application layer.

tips: Eliminate: B and D describe lower layers that map to the TCP/IP link, internet and transport layers.
Final two: C beats A because transport stays a separate layer in both models; only the top three OSI layers merge.
Exam cue: TCP/IP has four layers, and its application layer absorbs OSI layers 5 to 7, nothing below.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds Linux servers record administrator sign-ins but nothing of the actions taken once signed in. What should the auditor recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Log privileged commands with the individual user who ran them
options.B: Increase retention of the existing sign-in logs to two years
options.C: Require administrators to sign in from a dedicated network segment
options.D: Alert the security team whenever an administrator signs in

questions.key_concept: Logging must capture privileged actions tied to individual users, not only authentication events, to provide accountability.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the logs record and what they miss. Ask what an investigator would need after a harmful change.
questions.correct_explanation: Sign-in records show who accessed a server, not what they did there. Logging each privileged command with the individual user, for example through command logging or session recording, gives accountability for the actions most able to change systems and data. Alerting on administrator sign-ins adds visibility of access, but investigators still would not know which commands were run or what was changed.

wrong_explanations.B: Keeping sign-in logs longer preserves the same gap; they never recorded what administrators did.
wrong_explanations.C: A dedicated segment restricts where administrators connect from, not what they do once signed in.
wrong_explanations.D: An auditor would accept sign-in alerts as access monitoring, but an investigation reconstructs events, and an alert at the door says nothing about what happened inside.

tips: Eliminate: B extends logs that miss the actions, and C limits access paths without recording activity.
Final two: A beats D because command logging shows what administrators did; sign-in alerts only show that they arrived.
Exam cue: accountability needs logs of privileged actions tied to an individual, not just logs of sign-ins.

questions.question: A distributor's warehouse scanners use 300 wireless access points that all depend on one controller, so its failure would halt shipping. Which recommendation from the IS auditor would be MOST effective?

options.A: Add access points so their coverage overlaps across the warehouse
options.B: Pair the controller with a second unit that takes over automatically
options.C: Keep a preconfigured spare controller ready in the warehouse
options.D: Back up the controller's configuration to a secure server every night

questions.key_concept: A component every service path depends on is a single point of failure; redundancy with automatic failover removes it.
questions.pre_read: Ask which single part every access point depends on, and which option keeps service running without anyone acting.
questions.correct_explanation: The controller is a single point of failure for every access point, so the design needs a redundant partner. A second controller that takes over automatically keeps scanners connected when the first fails, with no one needing to act. A preconfigured spare speeds recovery, but someone must notice the failure, swap the hardware and bring it online, so shipping still stops in the meantime.

wrong_explanations.A: More access points add coverage, but every one still depends on the same controller, so its failure still stops them all.
wrong_explanations.C: A spare and a paired unit both answer controller failure, but the design question is who acts when it fails, and only one answer needs nobody.
wrong_explanations.D: A configuration backup helps rebuild a controller, but the single hardware dependency remains and shipping stops while it is replaced.

tips: Eliminate: A duplicates the access points, which are not the weak point, and D only speeds a rebuild after failure.
Final two: B beats C because automatic failover keeps shipping running; a spare still means an outage while it is installed.
Exam cue: find the component every path depends on; the strongest fix gives it a redundant partner that takes over automatically.

questions.question: A critical vendor security patch is available for production database servers. Which action should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST example of sound patch management?

options.A: Test it in staging, then deploy with a rollback plan
options.B: Upgrade to the next major database release instead
options.C: Apply it to the disaster recovery servers first as a test
options.D: Install it on production at once to close the exposure

questions.key_concept: Patch management applies vendor fixes on a managed schedule with testing, change control and rollback; urgency shortens testing but never removes it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh speed against the risk of an untested change. Ask what an emergency process still requires.
questions.correct_explanation: Patch management applies vendor fixes on a managed basis: assess, test in a representative environment, deploy through change control and keep a rollback plan. Even critical patches can break production systems. Installing at once closes the exposure fastest, but an untested patch on a production database can cause an outage worse than the vulnerability; urgent patches get expedited testing, not none.

wrong_explanations.B: A major version upgrade is a separate project with its own risks. It does not apply the vendor's security fix in a controlled way.
wrong_explanations.C: DR servers are not a test environment; a faulty patch there could leave the firm without recovery capability.
wrong_explanations.D: Emergency installs are a recognized path for exploited flaws, yet urgency compresses change control rather than suspending it.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps a fix for a risky upgrade, and C uses recovery servers as a test bed, risking the recovery capability.
Final two: A beats D because even critical patches need testing and rollback; urgency shortens the process but does not skip it.
Exam cue: change control applies even in emergencies; prefer expedited testing over untested deployment.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds each approved component of a payroll upgrade went live separately over three weeks, with no combined build, test or rollback plan. Which ITIL 4 practice is MOST clearly lacking?

options.A: Change enablement
options.B: Service continuity management
options.C: Service level management
options.D: Release management

questions.key_concept: Change enablement assesses and authorizes individual changes; release management coordinates packaging, testing and rollout of multiple changes.
questions.pre_read: Notice the changes were already approved. Ask which practice owns coordinating them into one release.
questions.correct_explanation: Release management plans and coordinates how a set of changes is packaged, tested and made available, including rollback. Here each change was approved, so change enablement worked as designed: it assessed risk and authorized each change individually. What was missing was the coordinated plan for deploying them together, which is the release management practice's job.

wrong_explanations.A: Change enablement did govern each component's risk and approval. A practice is lacking only where its own outputs are missing.
wrong_explanations.B: Service continuity management prepares for disaster recovery, not for how a set of changes is built, tested and rolled out.
wrong_explanations.C: Service level management agrees and tracks service targets; it does not plan deployments.

tips: Eliminate: B is about disaster recovery, and C is about agreed service targets, not deployments.
Final two: D beats A because the changes were already approved; packaging, testing and rolling them out together is release management's role.
Exam cue: change enablement authorizes individual changes; release management coordinates many changes into one planned, tested deployment.

questions.question: IT proposes a 99.999% availability target, with costly redundancy, for an internal expense-claims system. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Approve the target because higher availability lowers business risk
options.B: Benchmark the target against availability levels at peer firms
options.C: Fund the redundancy in phases over the next three years
options.D: Base the target on the system's business impact and tolerance

questions.key_concept: Availability targets derive from business impact and tolerance for downtime, so the cost of resilience matches business need.
questions.pre_read: Notice the system is internal and the target is extreme. Ask who should decide how available it must be.
questions.correct_explanation: Availability targets should come from business requirements, such as the impact of the expense system being down and how long users can tolerate it. Five nines for a noncritical internal process likely buys costly redundancy the business does not need. Benchmarking against peers gives useful context, but peers' targets reflect their own processes and risk appetite, not this system's actual business impact.

wrong_explanations.A: More availability is not automatically worth its cost; targets should match business need.
wrong_explanations.B: Peer benchmarks would help later, as a sanity check on an impact-based target; outside data calibrates a decision rather than making it.
wrong_explanations.C: Phasing spends the money more slowly but still assumes the target is justified.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes more availability is always worth paying for, and C phases spending on an unproven target.
Final two: D beats B because targets come from this system's business impact; peers' figures reflect their own needs.
Exam cue: availability and capacity targets are set by business requirements, then technology is sized to meet them.

questions.question: Some orders never reach the billing system, which receives them from the order system through data communications software. Which control should the IS auditor test FIRST?

options.A: Encryption settings on the billing database server
options.B: Posting-error logs in the billing batch job
options.C: User access rights in the order-entry application
options.D: Delivery acknowledgment and retry settings for messages

questions.key_concept: Data communications software manages sessions, routing and reliable delivery between systems; acknowledgments and retries control message loss.
questions.pre_read: Locate where the orders disappear. Ask which control operates at that point rather than before or after it.
questions.correct_explanation: Data communications software handles sessions, routing and delivery of messages between systems, so orders lost in transit point to its delivery controls. Acknowledgment and retry settings show whether undelivered messages are detected and resent. Billing posting-error logs are a natural place to look, but they record only messages that arrived; an order lost in transit never appears there.

wrong_explanations.A: Encryption protects stored data from disclosure; it does not affect whether messages arrive.
wrong_explanations.B: Posting-error logs do catch failures inside billing. Missing records point upstream, though: a gap with no error message usually means the data never arrived.
wrong_explanations.C: Access rights govern who can enter orders, not whether entered orders are delivered.

tips: Eliminate: A protects confidentiality, and C governs who may enter orders; neither affects delivery.
Final two: D beats B because orders lost in transit never reach billing, so its logs cannot show them.
Exam cue: match the control to where the failure occurs; delivery failures between systems point to the communications layer.

questions.question: Business analysts query the production database through one shared service account with broad rights. Which control should the IS auditor recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Encrypt the production database and its backups at rest
options.B: Provide monthly flat-file extracts for offline analysis
options.C: Issue named least-privilege accounts with audit logging
options.D: Rotate the shared service account password every quarter

questions.key_concept: Database access needs individual, least-privilege accounts with audit logging so every action is traceable to a person.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a shared account makes impossible, and which option restores it rather than hardening the shared credential.
questions.correct_explanation: A shared account with broad rights breaks individual accountability and least privilege: no one can tell which analyst ran a query or changed data. Individual accounts limited to the needed data, with database audit logging, restore both. Quarterly password rotation limits how long a leaked password works, but the account stays shared and over-privileged, so actions still cannot be traced to a person.

wrong_explanations.A: Encryption at rest protects stolen media, not misuse by users who connect legitimately through the account.
wrong_explanations.B: Extracts copy sensitive data outside database controls, widening exposure rather than fixing accountability.
wrong_explanations.D: An auditor would still expect a shared credential to be rotated. Rotation changes the secret, though, not how many people share it.

tips: Eliminate: A defends against stolen storage, not authorized misuse, and B spreads data outside the database's controls.
Final two: C beats D because individual accounts restore accountability, while rotating a shared password keeps every action anonymous.
Exam cue: shared privileged accounts are an accountability problem; prefer individual, least-privilege access with logging over tightening the shared credential.

questions.subtopic: Legacy Database Models. Hierarchical / Network Audit Considerations
questions.question: An IS auditor is planning a review of a payroll system that still runs on a hierarchical IMS database. Which consideration is MOST important?

options.A: Vendor support status and IMS skill availability
options.B: Running the standard relational audit program without modification
options.C: Testing the database for SQL injection flaws
options.D: The modernization timeline management has set for replacement

questions.key_concept: Legacy database risk centers on vendor support and scarce skills today; a future replacement plan does not reduce current exposure.
questions.pre_read: Ask what could make this system fail or go unsupported now, not what may happen after it is replaced.
questions.correct_explanation: For a legacy hierarchical database still running a critical process, the live risks are whether the vendor still supports the version in use and whether enough skilled staff remain to maintain and recover it. A modernization timeline matters for planning, but until replacement happens the system must keep running safely, and a date on a roadmap does not reduce today's support or skills exposure.

wrong_explanations.B: Relational audit programs assume SQL and normalized tables; hierarchical models need model-specific procedures.
wrong_explanations.C: IMS is not queried through SQL, so SQL injection tests miss the platform's actual risks.
wrong_explanations.D: An auditor uses the timeline to judge how long exposure lasts, but exposure has a size as well as a duration, and a timeline measures duration.

tips: Eliminate: B applies a relational program to a non-relational model, and C tests a SQL threat on a non-SQL database.
Final two: A beats D because current support and skills drive today's risk, while a future timeline does not reduce it.
Exam cue: for legacy platforms, focus on the risk of running them now, not on promises to replace them later.

questions.question: A critical ordering application fails completely whenever its payment gateway slows down. Which design change should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST fix?

options.A: Add a circuit breaker so payments degrade gracefully
options.B: Add more application instances behind the load balancer
options.C: Move the application onto one larger, faster server
options.D: Raise the gateway call timeout so slow replies can complete

questions.key_concept: A dependency failure cascades through every instance; circuit breakers and graceful degradation isolate it so the rest of the service survives.
questions.pre_read: Find where the failure starts. Then ask whether each option isolates that dependency or just adds capacity.
questions.correct_explanation: The failure starts in a slow downstream dependency and spreads because the application keeps waiting on it. A circuit breaker stops calls to the failing gateway and lets the rest of the application keep working in a reduced mode. Adding instances is a proven redundancy pattern, but every new instance calls the same slow gateway and fails the same way.

wrong_explanations.B: Extra instances work well when load is the bottleneck; a dependency that hangs needs a timeout and fallback designed in.
wrong_explanations.C: A single larger server adds a single point of failure and does nothing about the slow gateway.
wrong_explanations.D: Longer timeouts hold threads open longer, so requests pile up and the application fails sooner.

tips: Eliminate: C creates a single point of failure, and D makes calls wait longer on the slow gateway, so threads pile up.
Final two: A beats B because isolating the failing dependency stops the cascade; more instances inherit it.
Exam cue: match the resilience pattern to the failure mode; redundancy does not help when every copy shares the cause.

questions.question: Which DR test should the IS auditor recommend as MOST appropriate to prove the recovery site can process real transaction volumes without disrupting production?

options.A: A tabletop exercise walking through the recovery plan
options.B: A checklist review of the plan by each team lead
options.C: A full-interruption test shifting production to the recovery site
options.D: A parallel test processing live data at the recovery site

questions.key_concept: A parallel test proves the recovery site can process real workloads while production keeps running, unlike a full-interruption test.
questions.pre_read: Read the two conditions in the stem: real volumes and no disruption. Find the test that meets both.
questions.correct_explanation: A parallel test brings the recovery site up and runs real transactions through it while production continues, so it proves processing capability without risking live operations. A full-interruption test gives the strongest evidence, but it deliberately shuts down production and moves it to the recovery site, which breaks the stem's no-disruption condition and carries real business risk.

wrong_explanations.A: A tabletop exercise tests understanding of the plan through discussion; no systems process any transactions.
wrong_explanations.B: A checklist review confirms the plan's content and contacts but tests no processing capability at all.
wrong_explanations.C: An auditor values full interruption as the most demanding DR exercise, but test design starts from the limits the business sets, and disruption is ruled out.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are discussion and document tests that process no transactions.
Final two: D beats C because a parallel test proves capability while production keeps running; full interruption disrupts it.
Exam cue: real processing without production risk points to a parallel test; full interruption is for proven, mature plans.

questions.subtopic: Contractual Provisions for Alternative Processing Recovery
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a contract with a commercial hot-site vendor that serves many subscribers from one facility. Which provision is MOST important?

options.A: Monthly reporting on the vendor's own data center uptime
options.B: Priority rules for capacity when subscribers invoke together
options.C: A right to audit the vendor's physical and logical security controls
options.D: Discounted fees for subscribers signing multi-year terms

questions.key_concept: On a shared recovery site, the key contractual risk is contention, so capacity guarantees and priority rules for simultaneous invocations matter most.
questions.pre_read: Notice that the facility is shared. Ask what happens when a regional disaster hits several subscribers at once.
questions.correct_explanation: A shared hot site is oversubscribed by design, so the decisive risk is that several subscribers declare a disaster at the same time and capacity runs out. Guaranteed capacity and clear priority rules decide whether the firm can recover at all. A right to audit is a worthwhile provision, but good security at the site is worthless if the firm cannot get space there.

wrong_explanations.A: The vendor's normal uptime says nothing about whether capacity is available to this firm during a disaster.
wrong_explanations.C: A right to audit does give assurance over the vendor's controls, yet provisions rank by what they decide, and here that is access when demand peaks.
wrong_explanations.D: Fee discounts are a commercial term with no bearing on whether recovery will succeed.

tips: Eliminate: A measures the vendor's normal operations, not capacity in a shared disaster, and D changes the price, not any recovery obligation.
Final two: B beats C because contention for shared capacity decides whether recovery happens at all.
Exam cue: for shared or subscription recovery sites, look for capacity guarantees and priority during widespread events.

questions.question: A trade database has a 15-minute RPO and a four-hour RTO, but transaction logs are backed up only every four hours. What should the IS auditor report as the MOST significant gap?

options.A: Restoring the logs may take longer than the four-hour RTO
options.B: Committed trades since the last log copy could be lost
options.C: Log backups are not integrity-checked before storage
options.D: Weekly full backups lengthen the log restore chain

questions.key_concept: Backup or replication frequency must be at least as frequent as the RPO; otherwise the data loss window exceeds what the business accepted.
questions.pre_read: Separate the two objectives. RPO limits data loss; RTO limits downtime. Ask which one the log interval directly breaks.
questions.correct_explanation: The RPO says no more than 15 minutes of data may be lost, yet logs are captured only every four hours, so a failure could lose up to four hours of trades. That is a certain, measurable breach of the business requirement. Restore time against the RTO is worth testing, but nothing in the facts shows the RTO is missed, whereas the RPO gap follows directly from the schedule.

wrong_explanations.A: Restore timing does deserve a test, yet findings rest on what the facts show, and a schedule alone can prove a data-loss gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Nothing in the facts concerns log integrity; the stated gap is how often the logs are captured.
wrong_explanations.D: A long restore chain affects recovery time, which the facts do not show is breached; the certain gap is data loss.

tips: Eliminate: C raises integrity checks the facts never question, and D is a recovery-time worry while the schedule breaks the data-loss limit.
Final two: B beats A because the RPO breach is certain from the schedule, while an RTO breach is only a possibility.
Exam cue: compare backup frequency with the RPO and restore time with the RTO; never mix the two.

questions.question: An IS auditor must conclude whether last year's disaster recovery tests achieved recovery within the RTO. Which evidence is MOST reliable?

options.A: The approved test plan listing target recovery times
options.B: Timestamped system logs captured during the failover
options.C: A signed results summary confirming objectives were met
options.D: Participant interviews recalling how long recovery took

questions.key_concept: System-generated, contemporaneous evidence is more reliable than management assertions or recollection when testing whether recovery met its objective.
questions.pre_read: Rank the options by source: system-generated, management-prepared, or recalled. Then check which actually measures elapsed time.
questions.correct_explanation: Timestamped system logs created during the failover are objective, contemporaneous and generated independently of the people being assessed, so they directly show elapsed recovery time against the RTO. A signed results summary carries management accountability and is useful corroboration, but it is an assertion prepared after the event; the auditor still needs the underlying records to verify it.

wrong_explanations.A: A test plan records targets, not results. It cannot show what recovery time was actually achieved.
wrong_explanations.C: A signed summary is a valid management representation, but a signature shows who stands behind figures, not whether they are accurate.
wrong_explanations.D: Recollections a year later are subjective and imprecise. Oral evidence alone is the weakest form for timings.

tips: Eliminate: A shows only targets, not results, and D relies on memory, the weakest evidence for timing.
Final two: B beats C because system-generated records outrank a management assertion prepared after the event.
Exam cue: for evidence reliability, prefer independent, system-generated and contemporaneous records over statements.

questions.subtopic: Log Retention Gap During SEC Exam
questions.question: During a regulatory examination, the CISO learns IT shortened log retention below the legally required period without consulting compliance. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST next step?

options.B: Recover the purged logs from backups before anything else
options.C: Restore required retention and report the gap to management
options.D: Remind IT that retention changes need compliance sign-off

questions.key_concept: Stop a compliance gap growing first, then escalate it so management and counsel decide any disclosure; the auditor does not make that call.
questions.pre_read: Each day under the short setting purges more logs. Ask what stops the loss and who decides disclosure.
questions.correct_explanation: Every day the shortened setting stays, more required logs are purged, so retention must be restored at once and the gap reported to management, who decide with counsel how to inform examiners. Recovering purged logs from backups matters, but doing it first lets the loss continue, and backups may not hold everything, so stopping further loss comes first.

wrong_explanations.A: Involving compliance sounds prudent, but each day spent assessing lets the short setting purge more required logs; stop the loss first, then assess the exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Restoring purged logs from backup does recover some history. An open leak is closed before old damage is repaired, though, or the repair falls behind.
wrong_explanations.D: A reminder addresses how the change slipped through, yet the non-compliant setting keeps deleting required logs until someone restores the legal retention period.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because an exposure assessment and a staff reminder both leave the short setting purging required logs in the meantime.
Final two: C beats B because stopping further loss comes before recovering past data, and management must know now.
Exam cue: contain first, then remediate; disclosure to regulators is management's decision, informed by the auditor.

wrong_explanations.B: Release notes describe intended changes; they do not reveal a defect that silently drops records.

questions.question: A tape is missing from the offsite vault, and no one can show who held it between operators, couriers and the vault. Which control should the IS auditor recommend as MOST important?

options.D: A courier contract with liability for lost tapes

questions.correct_explanation: Without an acknowledged record at each transfer, a missing tape cannot be traced to the point or party where it went astray, and nobody is accountable. wrong_explanations.D: Liability compensates for a loss after it happens; it does not record who held which tape.

tips: Eliminate: C records only the vault end of the chain, and D compensates for losses without recording custody.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a Layer 3 switch routes traffic between cardholder-data and office networks without restriction. Which device would BEST enforce a security policy between the networks?

options.A: A load balancer spreading sessions across both networks
options.B: A separate Layer 2 switch for each of the networks
options.C: A firewall applying rule sets between the networks
options.D: A dedicated router forwarding packets between the networks

questions.key_concept: Routers and switches forward traffic; firewalls enforce security policy by permitting or denying flows according to rules.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each device is built to do. Which one decides whether traffic is allowed, not just where it goes?
questions.correct_explanation: A firewall's purpose is to enforce security policy, permitting only approved flows between zones and logging the rest, which is exactly what segmentation of cardholder data requires. A dedicated router is a common boundary device, but its main job is forwarding packets between networks. Replacing one routing device with another would still let traffic pass without policy enforcement.

wrong_explanations.A: A load balancer distributes traffic across a server pool for availability. It is not designed to enforce access policy between zones.
wrong_explanations.B: Layer 2 switches forward frames within a network. Adding them does not control the routed traffic between the two networks.
wrong_explanations.D: A router is fine for joining trusted segments; filtering is its sideline and a firewall's purpose, and cardholder segmentation needs the purpose-built control.

tips: Eliminate: A spreads load for availability rather than filtering flows, and B works within a network rather than between networks.
Final two: C beats D because a firewall enforces policy, while a router's core job is forwarding packets.
Exam cue: forwarding devices move traffic; when the question asks to enforce policy between zones, choose the firewall.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds several critical servers past vendor end-of-support, kept in service to save capital. Which risk should the auditor rate as GREATEST?

wrong_explanations.D: Rising energy use is an efficiency cost, minor beside unfixable flaws on servers running critical services.

questions.question: A capacity plan uses average monthly utilization of 55%, but month-end batch processing regularly saturates the servers. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

questions.pre_read: Notice the average looks comfortable while month-end fails. Ask what an average hides.
questions.correct_explanation: Averages hide the peaks that cause slowdowns and failures. Planning on peak demand, such as month-end, quarter-end and seasonal spikes, and their growth trends, sizes capacity for the periods the business depends on most. Alerting at 90% during month-end would confirm saturation as it happens, but it gives operators no time or resources to prevent it; it reports the problem rather than planning it away.

wrong_explanations.B: A month-end alert is sensible monitoring, though an alert that fires on schedule is a planning gap being reported, not managed.
wrong_explanations.D: Doubling an average is a guess that may overbuy or still miss the peak.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on an average that conceals the month-end peak, and D sizes capacity from the same misleading figure.
Final two: C beats B because planning for peaks prevents saturation; alerts only report it as it happens.

questions.question: A problem team's root cause analysis of a storage outage stops at 'operator error'. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Find why the process allowed the operator's error
options.B: Retrain the operator and close the problem record
options.C: Add a second operator to check each storage task
options.D: Automate restarts so the outage recovers faster next time

questions.key_concept: Root cause analysis should look past human error to the process, tool or procedure weaknesses that allowed it.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the analysis stopped. Ask whether 'operator error' explains why the outage could happen.
questions.correct_explanation: Human error is rarely a root cause; continuing the analysis asks why the process, tooling or procedures let the error happen, which finds the fix that stops anyone repeating it. Retraining the operator is a reasonable action, but closing the record on it treats the symptom and leaves the same trap for the next person.

wrong_explanations.B: Retraining is a normal corrective step. The strongest fixes change the system, though, so that no one can repeat the error.
wrong_explanations.C: A second checker is a fix chosen before the cause is known, and it may not address why the error was possible.
wrong_explanations.D: Faster recovery is a workaround that leaves the cause in place.

tips: Eliminate: C picks a control before the cause is known, and D speeds recovery without addressing cause.
Final two: A beats B because the systemic cause must be found; retraining one person treats a symptom.
Exam cue: when root cause analysis ends at human error, keep asking why the process allowed it.

questions.question: Service desk reports show 99% of tickets resolved within SLA, yet business users rate the service poorly. Which change should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Tighten resolution-time targets for every ticket priority
options.B: Report each technician's ticket count to management
options.C: Drop the targets the desk already meets consistently
options.D: Add satisfaction and repeat-incident measures to the SLA

questions.key_concept: Good SLA metrics balance speed with outcome and customer experience; when speed targets are met but users are unhappy, the metric set is incomplete.
questions.pre_read: Notice speed targets are met but users are unhappy. Ask what the current metrics are failing to measure.
questions.correct_explanation: Meeting speed targets while users are dissatisfied shows the metrics measure activity, not outcomes. Adding customer satisfaction and repeat-incident measures reveals whether tickets are truly resolved and whether users experience good service. Tightening resolution targets raises the bar, but it measures the same dimension more strictly and may push staff to close tickets faster without fixing them.

wrong_explanations.A: An auditor would accept tighter targets on a slow desk, but a metric set is fixed by adding what it misses, not tightening what it has.
wrong_explanations.B: Per-technician volume is a productivity statistic that says nothing about whether users' issues are solved.
wrong_explanations.C: Dropping met targets removes visibility of performance and does not explain the dissatisfaction.

tips: Eliminate: B measures individual output, and C removes visibility without explaining the gap.
Final two: D beats A because the gap is a missing outcome measure, not a speed target that is too loose.
Exam cue: when green metrics clash with unhappy users, the metric set is measuring the wrong thing.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds engineers make firewall rule changes directly in production and document them afterward. Which control is MOST important to recommend?

options.A: Back up firewall configurations to a secure repository
options.B: Maintain a CIO-approved diagram of the current network topology
options.C: Approve and test firewall rule changes before they are made
options.D: Review the firewall change logs each week for unauthorized edits

questions.key_concept: Network change control is preventive: rule changes are approved and tested before implementation, not just documented or reviewed after the fact.
questions.pre_read: Notice changes are documented only afterward. Ask which control acts before a bad rule reaches production.
questions.correct_explanation: Changes made first and documented later mean a flawed or unauthorized firewall rule takes effect before anyone checks it. Requiring approval and testing before implementation stops bad rules from reaching production. A weekly review of change logs adds detection, but a harmful rule could expose systems for up to a week before anyone notices, and the review depends on logs being complete.

wrong_explanations.A: Backups help recover a configuration, but they do not stop unapproved rule changes going live.
wrong_explanations.B: An approved diagram supports understanding of the network, not authorization of individual rule changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Prevent where one change can do harm at once. Weekly review would catch a bad rule, but no later check undoes exposure already suffered.

tips: Eliminate: A supports recovery, and B supports documentation; neither controls rule changes.
Final two: C beats D because approval before change prevents harm, while a weekly review finds it after the fact.
Exam cue: when changes are made first and recorded later, recommend the preventive approval step.

questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm the incident response process works in practice, not just on paper. Which evidence is MOST persuasive?

options.B: Timestamped records of recent incidents traced through each phase
options.C: Results of a tabletop exercise run by the response team
options.D: The response platform vendor's latest SOC 2 report

questions.key_concept: Operating effectiveness is shown by evidence of real execution: records of actual incidents traced through detection, containment, resolution and reporting.
questions.pre_read: Notice the words in practice. Ask which evidence shows the process actually ran on real events.
questions.correct_explanation: Operating effectiveness is best shown by what happened on real incidents. Tracing timestamped records of recent incidents through detection, containment, resolution and reporting shows whether each phase actually ran as designed and on time. A tabletop exercise is useful evidence of readiness, but it tests a simulated scenario in a discussion setting, so it is weaker than records of the process working under real conditions.

wrong_explanations.A: A policy shows design only; it gives no evidence that responders followed it on real incidents.
wrong_explanations.C: A tabletop is an established exercise where incidents are too rare to sample, but once a population of actual cases exists, the auditor tests from it.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor report covers the platform's controls, not how the firm's own team responded to incidents.

tips: Eliminate: A shows design only, and D covers the vendor rather than the firm's response.
Final two: B beats C because records of real incidents prove operation, while a tabletop only simulates it.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a procedure that lets on-call engineers deploy emergency fixes outside the change advisory board cycle. Which control is MOST important?

options.B: Independent review and approval of each change soon after deployment

questions.key_concept: Emergency changes may bypass prior approval but must receive independent review and approval soon after implementation.
questions.pre_read: Notice who deploys the change. Ask who, other than the implementer, confirms afterwards that it was justified.
questions.correct_explanation: Emergency changes skip normal approval, so control must return through independent review soon afterwards: someone other than the implementer confirms the change was needed, authorized and correctly made. Engineer documentation creates a record, but a record written by the person who made the change is self-review and gives no independent assurance that the change was appropriate.

wrong_explanations.A: Engineer write-ups belong in every emergency change record, but documentation answers what was done; review answers whether it should have been.
wrong_explanations.C: Requiring full prior change board approval defeats the purpose of an emergency path when production is down; control shifts to prompt review afterward.
wrong_explanations.D: Response time measures speed, not whether emergency changes were justified, authorized or correct.

tips: Eliminate: C holds every fix for full change board approval while production is down, and D measures speed rather than control.
Final two: B beats A because an independent reviewer gives assurance that the implementer's own record cannot.

questions.question: A newly formed crisis management team has never exercised the organization's continuity plan. Which exercise should the IS auditor recommend scheduling FIRST?

options.B: A tabletop walkthrough of roles and key decisions
options.C: A parallel test that runs systems at the recovery site
options.D: A vendor-run drill that the crisis team watches as observers

questions.key_concept: BCM exercises progress from tabletop to simulation, parallel and full-interruption tests, each building capability for the next.
questions.pre_read: Notice the team has never exercised. Ask which exercise builds understanding without putting systems at risk.
questions.correct_explanation: A team that has never exercised needs to learn its roles and decision points before systems are moved. A tabletop walkthrough does this safely and exposes gaps in the plan cheaply. A parallel test is a valuable later step, but running recovery systems with a team unsure of its roles wastes the test and adds operational risk.

wrong_explanations.A: A full interruption of production is the riskiest test and is used only after lower-level exercises have succeeded.
wrong_explanations.C: Parallel testing is the usual proof that recovery systems carry work, yet a first exercise should be the cheapest that exposes the most gaps.
wrong_explanations.D: Watching someone else's drill does not build the team's own decision-making or test its understanding of the plan.

tips: Eliminate: A risks production with an untrained team, and D leaves the team as spectators.
Final two: B beats C because exercises progress from discussion to live systems; the team must know its roles first.

questions.question: A critical vendor's SOC 2 Type II report has an unmodified opinion but lists exceptions in change-management controls the firm relies on. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Assess how the exceptions affect the firm's own audit risks
options.B: Ask the vendor for its plan to remediate the exceptions
options.C: Request the vendor's SOC 3 report for a clearer summary
options.D: Re-perform the service auditor's tests of change management

questions.key_concept: SOC report exceptions matter even under an unmodified opinion; the user auditor judges each against the controls the firm relies on.
questions.pre_read: Notice that the opinion is clean but the report lists exceptions. Ask what those exceptions mean for the firm's reliance.
questions.correct_explanation: An unmodified opinion means the controls broadly met their objectives, yet the report can still list exceptions found in testing. Because the firm relies on the vendor's change management, the IS auditor first assesses what those exceptions mean for the firm's own risks, such as whether user controls compensate or extra testing is needed. Asking for a remediation plan is the most tempting alternative: it matters, but it addresses future periods, not this one.

wrong_explanations.B: An auditor would ask for a remediation plan in time, but the user organization first judges what each exception means for its own reliance.
wrong_explanations.C: A SOC 3 report is a brief public summary without test details, so it would hide the exceptions rather than explain them.
wrong_explanations.D: Re-performing the service auditor's tests duplicates the work reliance is meant to avoid; the exceptions are already documented.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because a SOC 3 summary drops the test detail, and re-performing the tests duplicates work the report already documents.
Final two: A beats B because the exceptions' effect on the firm's reliance is judged first; a remediation plan addresses later periods, not this one.
Exam cue: an unmodified opinion can still list exceptions; read the tested controls and judge each exception against what you rely on.

questions.question: A cloud region outage is two hours old with 6–12 hours to restore against a four-hour RTO, and the BCP names the CIO as invocation authority. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Fail over workloads for the customers who are demanding it
options.B: Invoke failover now and brief the CIO once it completes
options.C: Escalate to the CIO now for an immediate failover decision
options.D: Escalate to the CIO after the provider's four-hour update

questions.key_concept: When an outage will exceed the RTO, the invocation decision must be made quickly by the authority the plan names.
questions.pre_read: Compare the provider's estimate with the RTO. Then check who the plan says makes the invocation decision.
questions.correct_explanation: The provider's estimate already exceeds the four-hour RTO, so a failover decision is needed now, but the BCP gives that decision to the CIO. Escalating immediately gets an authorized invocation within minutes. Invoking without the CIO relies on the team's own judgment, but it bypasses the plan's named authority, and failover commits cost and data-loss trade-offs that the plan reserves for that executive.

wrong_explanations.A: Choosing by which customers complain replaces the plan's business-impact priorities with pressure from the loudest voices.
wrong_explanations.B: An auditor would credit the aim of protecting the four-hour RTO, yet urgency shortens the route to an authority rather than transferring it.
wrong_explanations.D: By hour four the RTO has already passed, and failover still takes time. The current estimate is enough for the CIO to decide now.

tips: Eliminate: A lets customer pressure override the plan's priorities, and D waits until the RTO is already lost.
Final two: C beats B because the plan names the CIO as invocation authority, and escalating now costs minutes, not the RTO.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the asset inventory of a firm running workloads on three cloud providers. Which practice provides the MOST reliable inventory?

options.B: Monthly billing reports reconciled to cost-center codes
options.C: Asset records kept in each provider's native console

questions.pre_read: Think about how fast cloud resources change. Ask which source sees a new resource the moment it exists and knows who owns it.
questions.correct_explanation: Cloud resources are created and destroyed in minutes, so only continuous discovery through each provider's APIs keeps pace. Checking results against mandatory ownership tags turns a list of resources into an accountable inventory. Billing reports are tempting because they cover every paid service, but they lag, miss configuration detail and cannot say who owns or approved an untagged resource.

wrong_explanations.B: An auditor might use billing as a cross-check, yet an inventory is only as reliable as its freshness and its owners, and invoices supply neither.
wrong_explanations.C: Native consoles list resources per provider but give no single inventory or ownership view across the three clouds.

tips: Eliminate: A is a stale manual snapshot, and C leaves three separate views with no consolidated, owned inventory.
Final two: D beats B because continuous discovery with ownership tags is timely and accountable, while billing lags and cannot name owners.

questions.question: Only one engineer can restore the core payment platform. Which action should the IS auditor recommend to BEST address this workforce risk?

options.A: Cross-train a second engineer and rehearse the restore
options.B: Document the restore steps in a detailed runbook for others
options.C: Buy key-person insurance covering the engineer's absence
options.D: Outsource the platform restore to a managed service vendor

questions.key_concept: Single-person dependency is resolved by building tested capability in another person, not by documents, insurance or outsourcing alone.
questions.pre_read: Ask what would actually happen on the day the engineer is unavailable. Which option proves someone else can do the restore?
questions.correct_explanation: The risk is that recovery depends on one person. Cross-training a second engineer and rehearsing the restore creates proven, alternate capability, which ISO 22301 expects plans and people to demonstrate through exercises. A runbook is useful, but an untested document read for the first time during an outage often fails; it supports cross-training rather than replacing it.

wrong_explanations.B: A runbook is a worthwhile way to capture know-how, but a staffing risk is treated with staff: redundancy means a second engineer who has restored it.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance compensates financially but restores nothing. The platform still cannot be recovered when the engineer is absent.
wrong_explanations.D: Outsourcing moves the dependency to a vendor that does not yet know the platform, and the organization stays accountable for recovery.

tips: Eliminate: C only pays out money, and D shifts the dependency to an outsider who lacks platform knowledge.
Final two: A beats B because a rehearsed second person is tested capability, while a runbook alone is an untested plan.

questions.question: A BIA sets a four-hour RTO for customer support but not the level of service it must provide once resumed. What should the IS auditor recommend the BIA add as MOST important?

options.B: The minimum acceptable service level until normal operations return
options.C: The names of staff who will answer calls after recovery
options.D: The recovery strategy and alternate site the process will use

questions.key_concept: Alongside RTO and RPO, the BIA defines the minimum acceptable capacity (MBCO): the reduced service level acceptable until normal operations return.

questions.correct_explanation: An RTO says when a process must resume, but not how much of it. wrong_explanations.A: Full service at the four-hour mark would please customers most, yet recovery is priced by need, and the need on day one is smaller than normal.
wrong_explanations.C: Staff names belong in recovery plans and change often; the BIA defines requirements, not rosters.
wrong_explanations.D: Strategies are chosen after the BIA, from its requirements; the BIA defines what is needed, not how to provide it.

tips: Eliminate: C puts plan rosters in the BIA, and D picks a strategy, which comes after the BIA.
Final two: B beats A because the BIA defines the minimum acceptable service; demanding full service at once overstates the need.

questions.key_concept: Shadow AI is governed first by an acceptable-use rule for data in AI tools and a sanctioned alternative that meets the business need.
questions.pre_read: Notice why staff use the tool. Ask what happens to that need if the only response is a ban.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff use the tool because it meets a real need, so the first step is governance that covers both sides: a clear rule on what data may go into AI tools, and a sanctioned tool with proper data protections. Blocking public AI sites may help as a stopgap, but on its own, and made permanent, it pushes staff to personal devices, so the leakage continues out of sight.

wrong_explanations.B: An auditor would agree client data must stop leaving, yet a technical block is only as strong as staff's lack of alternatives.
wrong_explanations.C: Measuring and reporting usage has value later, but client data keeps leaving while the survey runs.
wrong_explanations.D: A free public tool usually offers no contractual deletion commitment, and asking does not stop further uploads.

tips: Eliminate: C studies the problem while data keeps leaving, and D relies on a provider with no contractual duty.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that customer records can be deleted while open orders still point to them, leaving orphan orders. Which database control is MOST LIKELY missing?

options.A: Entity integrity requiring a unique key for each customer
options.B: Referential integrity enforced between the two tables
options.C: Record locking during simultaneous updates to customer data
options.D: Nightly backups of the customer and order tables

questions.key_concept: Referential integrity makes every foreign key match an existing primary key, so linked records cannot be orphaned by deletes.
questions.pre_read: Decide whether the fault is inside one table or in the link between two tables, then pick the matching rule.
questions.correct_explanation: Referential integrity requires every foreign key, such as the customer number on an order, to match an existing primary key. Enforced in the database, it blocks deleting a customer who still has open orders, so orphans cannot arise. Entity integrity is a related rule, but it only makes each customer's own key unique and non-empty; it says nothing about records in other tables that point to it.

wrong_explanations.A: Entity and referential integrity both protect keys, yet each integrity rule governs one scope, a table's rows or the links between tables.
wrong_explanations.C: Locking prevents two users overwriting each other's changes at the same moment. It does not check links between tables.
wrong_explanations.D: Backups help recover lost data but do not stop the deletion that creates orphan orders.

tips: Eliminate: C handles simultaneous updates and D recovers data after the fact; neither checks links between tables.
Final two: B beats A because the fault is a broken link between tables; entity integrity covers only a table's own keys.
Exam cue: MOST LIKELY asks for the best-fitting cause; match the symptom, here a broken link between tables, to the control that governs it.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds the DR design replicates customer data nightly to a region where a data-localization law forbids storing any copy. What is the BEST recommendation?

options.B: Rely on the provider's contract for transfer compliance
options.C: Encrypt the replicated data in transit and at rest with customer-held keys
options.D: Move DR to a compliant region that still meets RTO and RPO

questions.key_concept: DR site selection must satisfy data residency rules and recovery objectives together; encryption does not change where data resides.
questions.pre_read: Notice what is prohibited: the location, not the exposure. Ask which option fixes the location without losing recovery capability.
questions.correct_explanation: Relocating the DR target to a compliant region removes the prohibited copies while keeping recovery capability, provided the new site is tested against the agreed RTO and RPO. Encryption with customer-held keys is a strong safeguard, but it does not change where the copies reside; a localization law that forbids storing data in a region applies however well the data is protected.

wrong_explanations.A: Stopping replication ends the transfer but leaves critical systems with no recovery path, trading a compliance breach for an unacceptable continuity gap.
wrong_explanations.B: A contract cannot override a localization law, and the organization stays accountable for where its customer data is stored.
wrong_explanations.C: Customer-held keys would settle a confidentiality rule; a localization law asks about place, not protection, and is met on its own terms.

tips: Eliminate: A removes recovery capability to solve a location problem, and B leans on a contract that cannot override the law.
Final two: D beats C because the location itself is prohibited; encryption protects the copies but they still reside there.
Exam cue: when a DR design breaks a constraint, redesign the site and re-prove RTO and RPO rather than dropping recovery.

options.B: Defer to the CISO's judgment on the report's sufficiency
options.C: Accept it once the complementary user entity controls are confirmed
options.D: Use it for provider reliance and test the firm's controls

questions.key_concept: A service provider's report covers the provider's controls; the firm's own program still needs separate audit evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose controls the report actually covers. Then ask what the audit committee believes it covers.
questions.correct_explanation: The report covers the provider's cybersecurity program, not the firm's. It supports reliance on the provider, but the firm's own program needs separate evidence. Confirming complementary user entity controls is a good reliance step, yet those controls cover only the firm's side of the outsourced service, not its whole cybersecurity program.

wrong_explanations.A: An unmodified opinion speaks only to the provider's subject matter. It says nothing about controls the firm itself operates.
wrong_explanations.B: The auditor must reach an independent conclusion on evidence sufficiency; deferring to the program owner impairs objectivity.
wrong_explanations.C: User entity controls are checked whenever a SOC report is relied on, yet no added step widens a provider's report to the user's program.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses a clean opinion with relevant scope, and B surrenders the auditor's independent judgment.
Final two: D beats C because user entity controls complete reliance on one service, not assurance over the whole program.

options.C: Sue for breach and withhold payments during the litigation

wrong_explanations.D: Planning a migration within the exit term is orderly, yet conceding a disputed term before testing it gives away leverage that cannot be won back.

tips: Eliminate: B cuts over without a tested migration, and C provokes a service stoppage mid-dispute.

questions.question: A firm closing a data center will sell its storage arrays to a reseller. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor that customer data was removed?

options.B: A clause in the reseller's contract requiring it to wipe every drive
options.C: Pre-handover sanitization certificates matched to inventory serial numbers
options.D: Photos of the arrays sealed and leaving the data center

questions.key_concept: Sanitize media before they leave the organization's control, and keep per-drive records reconciled to the asset inventory as evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option proves each drive was sanitized, and whether the data would leave the firm's control first.
questions.correct_explanation: Media should be sanitized, verified and recorded before they leave the organization's control. Certificates tied to drive serial numbers and reconciled to the asset inventory show that every drive was sanitized and none was missed. A contract requiring the reseller to wipe the drives is a useful control, but it is a promise rather than proof, and the data leaves the firm's control before any wipe happens.

wrong_explanations.A: Deleting volumes leaves data recoverable, and a staff statement is weaker evidence than records for each drive.
wrong_explanations.B: A wipe clause is a sensible reseller term, but outsourcing a task moves the work, not the firm's accountability for its data.
wrong_explanations.D: Photos show the arrays left the building, not that the data on their drives was removed.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on deletion, which leaves data recoverable, and D shows shipment rather than sanitization.
Final two: C beats B because per-drive records prove sanitization happened; a reseller's contract only promises it, after the data has left.

questions.question: A retailer has replaced its nightly backups with continuous replication to a distant data center. Which risk should the IS auditor report as MOST significant?

options.A: Operators may not yet know the new failover procedure
options.B: Corruption or ransomware would reach both copies at once
options.C: Replication traffic could slow the network during business hours
options.D: The distant site could lose the last few seconds of writes

questions.key_concept: Replication copies corruption and encryption within moments, so it never replaces isolated, point-in-time backups.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a near-instant copy carries besides good data, and what is left if both copies go bad.
questions.correct_explanation: Replication copies every change within moments, including deletions, corruption and ransomware encryption, so both copies can be ruined together and no clean restore point remains. Isolated, point-in-time backups are still needed. Losing the last few seconds of writes is the closest choice: replication over a long distance often carries that small window, but the loss is bounded and usually within the RPO, not the loss of every good copy.

wrong_explanations.A: A new procedure is learned through training and testing; the gap does not leave the retailer without a usable copy of its data.
wrong_explanations.C: Bandwidth affects performance and can be sized or scheduled; it does not threaten the retailer's ability to recover clean data.
wrong_explanations.D: Lost seconds and replicated corruption are both replication risks, but a live copy has no history, so it cannot return the firm to before the damage.

tips: Eliminate: A is a training gap and C a performance issue; neither leaves the retailer without a clean copy.
Final two: B beats D because a few lost seconds are a bounded loss, while copied corruption can ruin every recoverable version.
Exam cue: replication protects against site loss, not bad data; only isolated, point-in-time backups restore a clean state.

questions.question: Database logs show that the account of an analyst who only builds reports ran ALTER TABLE commands on the payroll schema. Which control weakness does this MOST LIKELY indicate to the IS auditor?

options.B: Structure-changing rights granted beyond what the role needs
options.C: No nightly full backup of the payroll tables
options.D: Missing referential integrity between the payroll tables

questions.key_concept: Structure-changing DDL rights belong to DBAs under change control; read-only roles should hold only the rights they need.
questions.pre_read: Identify what kind of command was run before deciding which control failed.
questions.correct_explanation: ALTER TABLE is a data definition language (DDL) command: it adds, drops or redefines fields and other structure, which only database administrators should do under change control. A report builder needs read access, so the account holds rights far beyond its role. Unapproved changes to payroll amounts come closest, but those would come from data manipulation commands such as UPDATE, not from ALTER TABLE.

wrong_explanations.A: Unapproved data fixes do threaten payroll, but evidence supports only the conclusions it can bear, and a structure change says nothing about stored values.
wrong_explanations.C: Backup frequency concerns recovery after loss; it does not explain how a reporting account could run structure-changing commands.
wrong_explanations.D: Referential integrity governs links between tables; its absence would not let an account run structure-changing commands.

tips: Eliminate: C is about recovering lost data and D about links between tables; neither explains how a reporting account could run these commands.
Final two: B beats A because ALTER TABLE redefines structure (DDL), while changing payroll amounts would need data manipulation (DML) commands.

Exam cue: data definition language (DDL) defines structure, data manipulation language (DML) manipulates data, data control language (DCL) controls access; match the command type before naming the weakness.

questions.question: A database server lost power with transactions in progress; its data files and transaction log are intact. Which recovery approach is MOST appropriate for the IS auditor to expect?

options.A: Restore last night's full backup, then roll the log forward
options.B: Reapply every logged change, whether finished or not
options.C: Rekey the day's entries from source documents
options.D: Undo unfinished work and redo committed work automatically

questions.key_concept: After a crash with intact data files, the database redoes committed work and undoes unfinished work from the log, without a restore.
questions.pre_read: First ask what was damaged: the running system or the stored data. The answer picks the recovery path.
questions.correct_explanation: A power loss leaves the data files intact, so the database recovers itself at restart. It reads the log, starting from the last checkpoint, redoes committed work from after-images and undoes unfinished work from before-images, keeping every committed transaction with the shortest outage. Restoring last night's backup and rolling forward is the closest choice: it reaches the same state, but it is the slower media-loss path and adds avoidable downtime.

wrong_explanations.A: Restore and roll forward is the standard media-recovery path, but the recovery method follows what was lost, and here the files survived the crash.
wrong_explanations.B: Reapplying unfinished work would commit half-done transactions, such as a debit without its credit, breaking atomicity.
wrong_explanations.C: Rekeying is slow and error-prone, and it is unnecessary when the log already holds every committed change.

tips: Eliminate: B would commit half-finished transactions, and C rekeys work the log already holds.
Final two: D beats A because intact data files need only a crash restart from the log; a full restore is the slower path for media loss.
Exam cue: a crash with intact files means undo uncommitted and redo committed work from the log; media loss means restore, then roll forward.

questions.question: A database with a 15-minute recovery point objective (RPO) copies its transaction log every 10 minutes to the same storage array as the database. Which risk is GREATEST for the IS auditor to report?

options.A: One failure destroying the database and its log copies
options.B: Ten-minute log copies falling short of the 15-minute target
options.C: Log copies competing with live transactions for array capacity
options.D: Log replay pushing recovery past the recovery time objective

questions.key_concept: Log copies meet the RPO only when stored apart from the database; one failure must not destroy both.
questions.pre_read: Check where a recovery copy is kept as well as how often it is made.
questions.correct_explanation: Ten-minute log copies meet the 15-minute RPO only if they survive the failure they guard against. On the same array, one failure destroys the database and its log copies together, so every change since the last backup is lost, far beyond the RPO. Replay time is the closest concern: it affects how long recovery takes, measured against a recovery time objective, not how much data survives.

wrong_explanations.B: Copies every 10 minutes are more frequent than the 15-minute RPO requires; the schedule is sound, but the storage location is not.
wrong_explanations.C: Capacity contention can slow transactions, but monitoring and capacity planning manage it; it does not threaten the ability to recover data.
wrong_explanations.D: Long log replay is a known threat to recovery time, but the stated target here measures data, and a slow recovery still recovers.

tips: Eliminate: B misreads the numbers, since 10-minute copies meet a 15-minute RPO, and C is a performance concern, not a recovery failure.
Final two: A beats D because the stated target is an RPO; one array failure loses the log copies with the database, while replay time affects only recovery time.
Exam cue: a backup or log copy stored with what it protects shares its fate; check where copies live, not only how often they run.

questions.subtopic: Storage Architecture. Resilience of a Shared SAN
questions.question: A storage area network serving 30 critical databases has dual controllers and RAID 6, but every server connects through one SAN switch. What is the GREATEST risk the IS auditor should report?

options.A: Two disks failing at once and breaking the RAID 6 set
options.B: One of the dual controllers failing and halting disk access
options.C: A disk rebuild slowing every database for several hours
options.D: A switch fault cutting all 30 databases off from storage

questions.key_concept: Resilience depends on every path: redundant controllers and disks still fail together behind a single shared switch.
questions.pre_read: Trace the path from server to disk and find any component with no backup.
questions.correct_explanation: Every server reaches the storage through one switch, so a single switch fault takes all 30 critical databases offline at once, despite the redundant controllers and disks. A disk rebuild comes closest: it is likely and slows service, but the databases keep running. Redundancy is only as strong as the weakest path, so the IS auditor reports the single switch with its business impact.

wrong_explanations.A: RAID 6 keeps data available through two simultaneous disk failures; it takes a third failure to lose data.
wrong_explanations.B: With dual controllers, the surviving controller takes over the workload, so one controller failure does not stop disk access.
wrong_explanations.C: A rebuild does slow the databases for hours, yet a slowdown is something users work through, and a lost storage path is something nobody works through.

tips: Eliminate: A is a double disk failure that RAID 6 survives, and B is a controller failure the second controller covers.
Final two: D beats C because a switch fault stops all 30 databases, while a rebuild only slows them.
Exam cue: redundant parts do not make a redundant path; find the one component every system passes through.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.14 (Redundancy of Information Processing Facilities); NIST SP 800-209 (Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure); ISO/IEC 27040 (Storage Security)

Public sources: ISO/IEC 27002, NIST SP 800-209, ISO/IEC 27040. questions.subtopic: Software Licensing. Moving to a Virtual Cluster
questions.question: A database licensed by the core was moved onto virtual machines spanning 20 hosts, and the vendor may charge for every physical core those hosts hold. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Buy core licenses covering every host the database might use
options.B: Confirm how the license counts cores in virtual environments
options.C: Move the database back to its original physical server
options.D: Cap each virtual machine at the licensed number of processors

questions.key_concept: License exposure depends on the license metric; confirm how the terms count virtualized cores before acting on a possible gap.
questions.pre_read: Note whether the deciding fact is known or still uncertain; uncertainty usually calls for confirming first.
questions.correct_explanation: The exposure depends on how the license terms count cores in a virtual environment, and the vendor may charge for every physical core on the 20 hosts. Confirming that rule first shows the true gap before money or effort is spent. Capping virtual processors is the closest choice: it helps only if the terms count virtual processors, which is exactly what is still unknown. Management then decides how to close any gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Buying for all 20 hosts before the counting rule is known may waste a large sum, or still miss the true metric.
wrong_explanations.C: Moving back disrupts operations and is premature; the actual exposure under the license terms is not yet known.
wrong_explanations.D: A processor cap is a familiar way to contain licensing costs, but the contract's counting rule, not the technical setup, sets the bill.

tips: Eliminate: A commits a large spend and C disrupts operations, both before anyone knows a shortfall exists.
Final two: B beats D because a virtual-processor cap helps only if the terms count virtual processors, and that is still unknown.
Exam cue: in license questions, confirm the metric and the true gap before buying, moving or reconfiguring anything.

Public sources: ISO/IEC 19770-1, COBIT 2019, ITIL 4.

questions.subtopic: Batch Recovery. Rerun After a Corrupt Checkpoint
questions.question: A billing batch failed midway after posting part of the run, and its checkpoint file is corrupt, so operators plan to rerun the job from the beginning. What should the IS auditor confirm FIRST?

options.A: The aborted run's partial postings have been backed out
options.B: The billing owner has approved the rerun in writing
options.C: Billing totals will be reconciled with the ledger afterward
options.D: The rerun is moved to staffed business hours instead

questions.key_concept: A rerun from the beginning is safe only after the failed run's partial updates are reversed or its files restored.
questions.pre_read: Check what the failed job already changed before deciding how to recover it.
questions.correct_explanation: Records posted before the failure are already in the billing files, so a rerun from the beginning would post them again unless those partial updates are reversed or the files restored first. Reconciling totals afterward is the strongest alternative: it would reveal duplicate bills, but only after customers may have received them. When recovering a batch, prevention comes before detection.

wrong_explanations.B: Approval authorizes the rerun but does not stop it posting the same records a second time.
wrong_explanations.C: A post-run reconciliation is a standard billing control, but a restart from the top is safe only on clean ground, and the aborted run left postings.
wrong_explanations.D: Running in business hours changes who is present, not whether the rerun posts records twice.

tips: Eliminate: B authorizes the rerun without protecting the data, and D only changes when it runs.
Final two: A beats C because backing out partial updates prevents double billing; reconciling afterward only detects it.
Exam cue: before any rerun from the start, ask what the failed run already posted and whether it was reversed.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 DSS01 (Managed Operations); COBIT 2019 DSS06 (Managed Business Process Controls)

questions.subtopic: RPA. Risks in an Unattended Payment Bot
questions.question: One unattended bot uses a single identity to create supplier payments and approve them for release. What is the GREATEST risk the IS auditor should report?

options.A: Wrong or misused payments released with no second check
options.B: Bot-released payments that cannot be traced to an accountable person
options.C: Supplier bank details exposed in the bot's activity logs
options.D: Bot software license costs rising as payment volume grows

questions.key_concept: Segregation of duties applies to bots: one identity should not both create and approve the same payment.
questions.pre_read: Identify which duties the single identity combines, then ask what that combination lets go unchecked.
questions.correct_explanation: When one identity both creates and approves payments, no second party checks either step, so a faulty rule, a tampered script or misuse of the bot's credential releases payments unchallenged. Segregation of duties applies to bots as it does to people. Weak traceability comes closest: it slows investigation after the fact, but the combined duties are what let wrong payments leave unchecked.

wrong_explanations.B: Untraceable bot activity is a real accountability gap, but payment controls are judged by what they let through, and nothing sits between creation and release.
wrong_explanations.C: Nothing in the stem suggests logging bank details; the stated weakness is one identity holding conflicting duties.
wrong_explanations.D: Licensing cost is a budgeting matter; it does not threaten the integrity of payments.

tips: Eliminate: C invents a logging problem the stem does not raise, and D is a cost concern, not a control risk.
Final two: A beats B because conflicting duties let wrong payments leave; weak traceability only hampers investigation afterward.
Exam cue: apply segregation of duties to bots as to people; one identity creating and approving the same transaction is the red flag.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.3 (Segregation of Duties); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties); COBIT 2019 DSS06 (Managed Business Process Controls)
